Senses.PreferredTarget: a silver mountain and iron wall
AlternateTargets: like a silver mountain and iron wall
Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'a silver mountain and iron wall.' The compound occurs 317 times in 142 allowed texts; 53 occurrences say 'like a silver mountain and iron wall' (如銀山鐵壁), and 21 use the exact longer comparison ending in 'resembling' (銀山鐵壁相似). Foyan asks, 'What is a silver mountain and iron wall?' (如何是銀山鐵壁) and answers, 'originally it is an affair inside one's own house' (元來是自家屋裏事); the same passage says that before he understood, it was like a silver mountain and iron wall, and after understanding, 'originally I am the iron wall' (元來我是鐵壁). Xueyan records cases 'without a route of meaning, like a silver mountain and iron wall' (無義路如銀山鐵壁者), and separately quotes Baiyun Duan: 'an inherited word or half-phrase not yet passed through is like a silver mountain and iron wall; once passed through, originally oneself is the silver mountain and iron wall' (從上留下一言半句未透者，如銀山鐵壁。及乎透了，元來自己便是銀山鐵壁). Zhongfeng applies the comparison when the words 'life and death' stop someone and says that 'impermanence of life and death, silver mountain and iron wall' are all present in Zhaozhou's question. A verse also records 'with one press, the silver mountain and iron wall collapse' (一拶銀山鐵壁摧).
Senses.Note: The corpus uses the compound as an image, a direct question, a self-report, a quotation about inherited sayings, and a verse. It can be something not passed through, something that collapses, or—according to Foyan and the Baiyun quotation—oneself after passing through. Those attested predicates are retained without replacing the image with an abstract interpretation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 且如何是銀山鐵壁元來是自家屋裏事
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Ancient Worthies Record, 'Longmen Foyan's Record, part seven.' Foyan asks, 'What is the silver mountain and iron wall?' and immediately says, 'Originally it is an affair inside one's own house.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 無義路如銀山鐵壁者，又却都會不得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xueyan Zuqin's own general address. He distinguishes old cases with a route of meaning from those 'without a route of meaning, like a silver mountain and iron wall,' which he says he could not understand.

Occurrences.Kwic: 從上留下一言半句未透者，如銀山鐵壁。及乎透了，元來自己便是銀山鐵壁。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xueyan's general address quotes Baiyun Duan: an inherited word or half-phrase not yet passed through is like the silver mountain and iron wall; once passed through, oneself is it. MasterName keys the containing speaker, while the note preserves the quoted source.

Occurrences.Kwic: 但是說著箇生死。如撞著銀山鐵壁相似一礙礙住。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng's instruction to five elders: when 'life and death' is mentioned, it is 'like colliding with a silver mountain and iron wall' and being stopped. This records the simile's verbal deployment.

Occurrences.Kwic: 生死無常銀山鐵壁。盡在此問處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng, instruction to Zongyu, comments on Zhaozhou's recorded 'the myriad things return to one' question: 'impermanence of life and death, silver mountain and iron wall—these are all in this question.'

The Linked-Pearls Collection of Verses on Old Cases records the verse line, 'with one press, the silver mountain and iron wall collapse.' The nearby broad compilation head does not safely identify the verse author, so MasterName is null.

Senses.PreferredTarget: snow heaped in a silver bowl
AlternateTargets: a silver bowl filled with snow
Senses.Explanation: Literally, "snow heaped in a silver bowl." In the founding public exchange, a monk asks Baling, "What is the school of Kanadeva?" and Baling answers with this phrase (如何是提婆宗？銀碗裏盛雪). The record preserves it as one of Baling's three turning phrases, alongside answers about the sharpest sword and the eye of the true teaching; Yunmen says that raising those three phrases is enough to repay Baling. Later masters continue to quote, question, and redeploy the exact wording. Tianyin quotes the answer while addressing his assembly, while Dayu sets "mountains are mountains, waters are waters—a silver bowl filled with snow" against "mountains are not mountains, waters are not waters—washing charcoal in ink" (山是山、水是水，銀碗裏盛雪；山不是山、水不是水，墨汁裏洗炭). The distinctive Chan deployment is the phrase's life as Baling's answer and a quotable turning phrase in later public teaching. The texts leave the concrete phrase without a further explicit gloss, and so does this entry.
Senses.Note: Attested 15 times in 14 allowlisted texts. The founding answer, later quotation, paired contrast, and free redeployment all refer to the same spoken image; no different thing or master-specific sense was found.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問巴陵：「如何是提婆宗？」陵曰：「銀碗裏盛雪。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The founding public exchange: asked about the school of Kanadeva, Baling answers, snow heaped in a silver bowl.

Occurrences.Kwic: 復舉：「巴陵鑒禪師，有僧問：『如何是提婆宗？』陵云：『銀碗裏盛雪。』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xueguan later raises Baling's answer as part of the three-turning-phrase case.

Occurrences.Kwic: 憶昔當時僧問巴陵：『如何是提婆宗？』陵云：『銀碗裏盛雪。』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Tianyin quotes Baling's public answer while addressing his assembly.

Occurrences.Kwic: 辨得即山是山、水是水，銀碗裏盛雪；辨不得山不是山、水不是水，墨汁裏洗炭。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dayu redeploys the phrase in a text-drawn contrast with washing charcoal in ink.

Occurrences.Kwic: 銀碗裏盛雪也好，秤錘裏掜汁也好，破沙盆裏煬羹也好
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yezhu lists the phrase alongside other concrete images before setting the whole list aside for his question.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the gate and courtyard — a teaching house's frontage and its approach
Senses.Explanation: Literally the gate and courtyard (門庭) at the front of a house; in the records, the frontage and distinctive approach of a teaching house. It is used for establishing a house in the forms 'set up a gate and courtyard' (立門庭, 79 occurrences), 'each set up a gate and courtyard' (各立門庭, 20), and 'establish a gate and courtyard' (建立門庭, 25). The common compound 'arrangements at the gate and courtyard' (門庭施設) occurs 180 times in 92 texts. The texts themselves set these outer arrangements against the inner hall and the upward road: one passage says that this is still an affair at the edge of Shouchang's gate-and-courtyard arrangements and that the honored upward road is separately distinguished (此猶是壽昌門庭施設邊事，須知向上一路尊貴自別); another says that this is still a small wonder among the gate-and-courtyard arrangements and has no connection at all with a patch-robed monk's own share (此猶是門庭施設小不思議，衲僧分中了無交涉). A house's demanding style is described as 'high and steep at the gate and courtyard' (門庭高峻, 34 occurrences) or 'solitary and steep at the gate and courtyard' (門庭孤峻, 44). The headword occurs 1,462 times in 291 allowlist texts.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense. The record itself contrasts the arrangements at the gate and courtyard (門庭施設) with the inner hall (堂奧) and the upward road (向上一路).

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of Guiding Principles from the Patriarchs (列祖提綱錄), guiding principles for the evening informal convocation (當晚小參提綱). The line says that divisions and branches each establish their own gate and courtyard (分宗列派，各立門庭).
Complete Book of the Five Lamps (五燈全書), entry for Chan Master Shangfeng Huihe (上封慧和禪師). It calls the arrangements at the gate and courtyard something used to deceive children (門庭施設，誑謼小兒).

Occurrences.Kwic: 此猶是壽昌門庭施設邊事，須知向上一路尊貴自別。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Complete Record of Chan Master Juelang Daosheng of Tianjie (天界覺浪盛禪師全錄), hall address on the master's birthday (師誕日上堂). The text contrasts affairs at the edge of Shouchang's gate-and-courtyard arrangements (壽昌門庭施設邊事) with the upward road (向上一路).

Occurrences.Kwic: 此猶是門庭施設小不思議，衲僧分中了無交涉。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Extensive Record of Chan Master Wuyi Yuanlai (無異元來禪師廣錄), recorded sayings at Baolin Chan Temple on Mount Dayang (住大仰寶林禪寺語錄). It calls the gate-and-courtyard arrangements a small wonder with no connection to a patch-robed monk's own share (門庭施設小不思議，衲僧分中了無交涉).

Occurrences.Kwic: 其奈門庭高峻，波瀾浩大。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Sanyi Yu (三宜盂禪師語錄), recorded sayings at old Zhuming Temple (住古朱明寺語錄). The expression 'high and steep at the gate and courtyard' (門庭高峻) describes a house's demanding frontage.
